engine_rules.name: Higher-string crossing demands down-stroke
engine_rules.falsifier: A phrase that ascends to a higher string and begins on an up-stroke violates this rule
engine_rules.anchor: When going to a higher string, use a down-stroke.

engine_rules.name: Lower-string crossing demands up-stroke
engine_rules.falsifier: A phrase that descends to a lower string and begins on a down-stroke violates this rule
engine_rules.anchor: When going to a lower string, use an up-stroke.

engine_rules.name: Same-string playing uses alternate strokes
engine_rules.falsifier: Consecutive same-direction strokes on one string for rhythmic accent (Chapter 9) override this rule
engine_rules.anchor: When playing on one string, use alternate strokes.

engine_rules.name: Directional picking minimizes pick travel distance
engine_rules.preference: always choose the stroke direction that requires the shortest pick arc
engine_rules.falsifier: Strict alternate picking on a string crossing is a concrete counter-example where travel distance is not minimized
engine_rules.anchor: I found one concept or rule that causes the pick to travel the least amount of distance.

engine_rules.name: Picking motion originates from elbow not wrist
engine_rules.falsifier: Wrist-rotation picking is a concrete counter-example that violates this rule
engine_rules.anchor: The movement should come from the elbow.

engine_rules.name: Right-hand fingers must not contact strings bridge or guitar body
engine_rules.falsifier: Anchoring pinky on the guitar body is a concrete counter-example
engine_rules.anchor: Do not touch the strings, bridge or any other part of the guitar with the fingers of your right hand.

engine_rules.name: Wrist and elbow must remain relaxed and non-tense
engine_rules.falsifier: A tense or tilted wrist during fast passages is a concrete violation
engine_rules.anchor: The right hand, wrist and elbow should always be relaxed and never tense or tight. The wrist should not move or tilt.

engine_rules.name: Every exercise must be practiced from both down-start and up-start
engine_rules.preference: only a very slight difference in sound should exist between the two starts
engine_rules.falsifier: Drilling only down-start version of an exercise violates this rule
engine_rules.anchor: I recommend that you practice all the exercises starting with both strokes. There should be only a very slight difference in sound.

engine_rules.name: Practice metronome range is MM 60 to 120 before increasing
engine_rules.preference: begin at MM 60, increase incrementally to 120 before pushing beyond
engine_rules.falsifier: Beginning practice above MM 120 skips the prescribed foundational tempo range
engine_rules.anchor: I recommend you practice these exercise at MM 60 to 120, then increase your speed from there.

engine_rules.name: Exercises must be studied in sequential order without skipping
engine_rules.falsifier: Opening the book to Chapter 5 arpeggios before completing Chapters 2-4 violates the stated sequence
engine_rules.anchor: The exercises are designed to take the student from point A to Z. It is not a good idea to skip around in this book

engine_rules.name: Up-stroke must sound as strong and round as down-stroke
engine_rules.preference: accent on upstroke should equal downstroke volume and tone
engine_rules.falsifier: An upstroke that sounds weaker or thinner than the downstroke is a concrete violation
engine_rules.anchor: The goal is to make the up-stroke sound as strong and round as the down-stroke.

engine_rules.name: Wrist must be straight but not stiff during picking
engine_rules.falsifier: A locked stiff wrist or a bent wrist both violate this rule
engine_rules.anchor: Practice keeping your wrist straight but not stiff. Remember: the movement is from the elbow.

engine_rules.name: Proscription: do not anchor fingers on pick guard or strings
engine_rules.falsifier: Resting any finger on the pick guard during an exercise is a concrete violation
engine_rules.anchor: Do not touch the pick guard or strings with the fingers of the right hand.

engine_rules.name: In-between stroke requires complete note separation — no ringing
engine_rules.preference: take extra time mastering this stroke before moving forward
engine_rules.falsifier: Allowing adjacent-string notes to sustain together during the in-between stroke violates this rule
engine_rules.anchor: Do not let notes ring!

engine_rules.name: In-between stroke is the most difficult stroke in the system requiring most practice attention
engine_rules.preference: take your time with this one
engine_rules.anchor:
This is the hardest stroke to master. It involves going between two adjacent strings.
            This is a critical part of your right hand technique. Take your time with this one.

engine_rules.name: Consecutive same-direction strokes across adjacent strings require no ringing
engine_rules.falsifier: Allowing two adjacent-string notes to sustain simultaneously during a consecutive sweep is a concrete violation
engine_rules.anchor: Do not let notes ring!

engine_rules.name: Rhythmic precision of eighth notes takes priority over tempo increase
engine_rules.preference: evenness is the prerequisite; speed follows
engine_rules.falsifier: Increasing metronome tempo before achieving even note durations violates this rule
engine_rules.anchor:
It is necessary to play the above exercises evenly . At this stage, precision of the 8th
   notes is more important than speed.

engine_rules.name: Repeating triplet patterns in exercises use three downs then three ups
engine_rules.preference: three consecutive strokes same direction across three adjacent strings
engine_rules.falsifier: Using strict alternate picking for a triad triplet exercise is the counter-example this rule overrides
engine_rules.anchor:
use three "down-strokes" followed by three "up-strokes". Apply to any three note chord on
     any three adjacent strings.

engine_rules.name: Triplet exception is exercise-only — real melodic lines adhere to the main directional rule
engine_rules.preference: in a real phrase context, revert to higher-string/lower-string directional rule
engine_rules.falsifier: Applying the three-down/three-up exercise pattern within a bebop melodic line would be the violation
engine_rules.anchor:
however, if I had to play a triplet phrase in the context of a line and not in an exercise,
             I would adhere to the rule.

engine_rules.name: Repeated notes on the same string require a pick-direction reversal
engine_rules.falsifier: Playing two consecutive repeated notes with the same stroke direction on one string violates this rule
engine_rules.anchor: This exercise requires you to reverse direction on the same string. A common stroke that happens with

engine_rules.name: Directional picking rule applies uniformly to all scale fingerings and scale-type passages
engine_rules.falsifier: Applying strict alternate picking to a scale passage ignores this generalization
engine_rules.anchor:
This will give you an idea how the rule works
           on any sclae or scale type passage..

_provenance.section_title: Picking rule generalizes to all scales

engine_rules.name: Double-star notation marks higher-string crossing requiring down-stroke
engine_rules.falsifier: A ** marking without a down-stroke is a notation-rule violation
engine_rules.anchor: ** = moving to HIGHER STRING

engine_rules.name: Single-star notation marks lower-string crossing requiring up-stroke
engine_rules.falsifier: A * marking without an up-stroke is a notation-rule violation
engine_rules.anchor: * = moving to LOWER STRING

engine_rules.name: Arpeggio articulation takes priority over tempo
engine_rules.preference: never increase tempo until note separation is clean
engine_rules.falsifier: Speeding through an arpeggio exercise with ringing notes violates this rule
engine_rules.anchor:
Articulatioin is more important
    han speed.

engine_rules.name: Sweep picking is not a separate technique — the directional rule unifies single-line and arpeggio picking
engine_rules.preference: reject any framing that treats arpeggios as requiring a different picking system
engine_rules.falsifier: Treating sweep picking as a separate learned skill contradicts this rule
engine_rules.anchor:
I see no reason to make any distinction. Everything follows the rule:
      Higher string = "down stroke" Lower string = "up stroke"

engine_rules.name: Minor 11 fingering enables sextuplet via consecutive strokes across four strings
engine_rules.preference: choose the fingering that places six notes across four adjacent strings
engine_rules.falsifier: A minor 11 fingering that does not span four strings cannot produce the sextuplet pattern
engine_rules.anchor:
Minor 11 arpeggios: Because of the fingering it is possible to play 6 notes in one beat.(sextuplet)
      The fingering sets up the consecutive down and up strokes to go across four strings.

engine_rules.name: Minor 9 arpeggio fingering places notes on adjacent strings to enable two-octave fluid picking
engine_rules.preference: use fingerings that keep successive arpeggio notes on adjacent strings
engine_rules.falsifier: A minor 9 fingering with string skips between every note cannot apply the adjacent-string consecutive rule
engine_rules.anchor:
Minor 9th arpeggios:By using fingerings that place notes on adjacent strings, either higher or lower,
       these large two octave arpeggios become possible.

engine_rules.name: Fingering choice is the primary mechanism enabling arpeggio speed
engine_rules.preference: optimize the left-hand fingering before trying to pick faster
engine_rules.falsifier: Attempting to increase arpeggio speed by picking harder without changing fingering violates this principle
engine_rules.anchor:
Again, the fingering makes
      the speed possible.

engine_rules.name: After a rest between phrases either stroke may begin the next phrase
engine_rules.preference: use whichever stroke feels natural after the rest
engine_rules.anchor:
I have found when there is a rest between phrases,
        it is possible to break the rule and use whatever stroke you
        please to start the phrase.

_provenance.section_title: Rule exception at rests and practice symmetry

engine_rules.name: Single-line and arpeggio picking are governed by one system not two
engine_rules.preference: reject the misconception that arpeggios require a different picking approach
engine_rules.falsifier: Treating single-line picking and arpeggio picking as separate skills is the misconception this rule addresses
engine_rules.anchor:
I often run across guitarists
     who become misled into thinking that picking for single lines is different than picking for arpeggios.

_provenance.section_title: Rule exception at rests and practice symmetry

engine_rules.name: Musical intent governs picking choices — fretboard must not dictate the music
engine_rules.preference: always subordinate mechanical efficiency to musical expression
engine_rules.falsifier: Choosing a musical phrase solely because it is easy to pick on the fretboard is the named anti-pattern
engine_rules.anchor:
You have to be careful
     to NOT let the fingerboard make the music. The music comes from inside; the picking mechanism described in this book
     is designed to make it easier for the music to be realized.

engine_rules.name: Major triad arpeggio exercise serves as foundational warm-up for note separation
engine_rules.preference: use this exercise daily to develop note separation transferable to all arpeggio fragments
engine_rules.falsifier: Skipping the major triad warm-up and moving directly to complex arpeggios skips the articulation foundation
engine_rules.anchor:
This makes a great warm-up exercise. It is very difficult to
     play with clean articulation.

engine_rules.name: Directional picking rule applies to non-adjacent string crossings identically to adjacent crossings
engine_rules.falsifier: Using strict alternate picking for a string skip because strings are non-adjacent violates this extension
engine_rules.anchor:
When skipping strings the same rule applies: When going to a higher string use a
          down-stroke; when going to a lower string, use an up-stroke.

engine_rules.name: String-skip exercises must be started with both down and up strokes
engine_rules.falsifier: Practicing a string-skip exercise only from a down-start violates this symmetry requirement
engine_rules.anchor: START THIS EXERCISE WITH BOTH STROKES, DOWN AND UP

engine_rules.name: Up-stroke accent with string skip may pragmatically use alternate picking
engine_rules.preference: author finds alternating down-up easier for accented in-between skip figures
engine_rules.falsifier: Successfully executing the accented in-between skip with the directional rule removes the need for this preference
engine_rules.anchor:
I find that when playing exercises like this it is easier to play them
     with alternating "down" - "up" strokes

_provenance.section_title: Accent on up-stroke skip — pragmatic alternate preference

engine_rules.name: Changing fingerboard position of a phrase changes its required picking pattern
engine_rules.preference: do not assume the same picking applies when a phrase moves positions
engine_rules.falsifier: Applying the same picking pattern to a phrase transposed to a new position without re-deriving it from the directional rule is the named error
engine_rules.anchor: Here's the same phrase in the 7th position. This changes the picking considerably.

engine_rules.name: Slurred triplets are preferred over fully-picked triplets for bebop phrasing
engine_rules.preference: prefer the slurred example as it sounds more horn-like
engine_rules.falsifier: Picking every triplet note fully with no slur produces the less preferred, less horn-like sound
engine_rules.anchor: I prefer the 2nd example; it sounds more horn-like

engine_rules.name: Slurred triplet figures must be mastered starting from both down and up strokes
engine_rules.falsifier: Mastering only the down-stroke start for slurred triplets leaves the up-stroke variant unpracticed
engine_rules.anchor: Learn how to slur triplets with a "down-stroke" and an "up-stroke"

engine_rules.name: Slurring is mechanically defined as one pick stroke producing two sounded notes
engine_rules.falsifier: Picking both notes individually produces two attacks and is not a slur
engine_rules.anchor:
These inflections are accomplished
     by slurring notes. Pick one note and play two notes.

engine_rules.name: Slurs are physically constrained to note pairs on the same string
engine_rules.falsifier: Attempting a hammer-on or pull-off between notes on different strings is not possible on guitar
engine_rules.anchor: Try moving the slur over any two notes that are on the same string.

engine_rules.name: Shifting slur position within a phrase changes its expressive inflection
engine_rules.preference: experiment with placing slurs at different beats to discover expressive alternatives
engine_rules.falsifier: Fixing the slur always on the first note of every phrase eliminates this expressive resource
engine_rules.anchor: Here is the phrase with the slur moved to the next beat.

engine_rules.name: Bebop phrase endings should be played long then short
engine_rules.preference: the two final notes of a bebop phrase should be long followed by short
engine_rules.falsifier: Playing both final notes with equal duration omits the idiomatic long-short gesture
engine_rules.anchor:
make sure you play these last two notes,
                                                             long, short.

engine_rules.name: Students should actively experiment adding slurs at different phrase positions
engine_rules.preference: do not treat slur placement as fixed; internalize it as a creative choice
engine_rules.falsifier: Copying only the notated slur placements without exploring alternatives limits expressive range
engine_rules.anchor: I've added a few slurs. Experiment adding your own slurs at different places

engine_rules.name: Consecutive down-strokes are permitted to emphasize notes in big-band style phrases
engine_rules.preference: use when emulating horn-section accent patterns
engine_rules.falsifier: Applying consecutive downs in a lyrical bebop ballad context where accent imitation is not the goal would be misapplied
engine_rules.anchor:
I use consecutive down strokes to emphsis certain notes. This type picking is useful when you
    are trying to emulate a big band type phrase.

engine_rules.name: A rhythmic break or rest between notes justifies consecutive down-strokes
engine_rules.preference: use two downs when a rest separates notes rather than forcing directional-rule alternation
engine_rules.falsifier: A continuous melodic line without rests does not provide the rhythmic gap that licenses this exception
engine_rules.anchor: When there is a rhythmic break between notes, you may want to use to down strokes.

engine_rules.name: Slurs are an equivalent alternative to consecutive down-strokes for big-band phrasing
engine_rules.preference: slurs and consecutive downs are interchangeable expressive options for this context
engine_rules.falsifier: Treating consecutive downs as the only option for big-band phrases ignores the slur alternative
engine_rules.anchor: Here is the same type phrase with slurs.

engine_rules.name: Repetition without mid-stroke analysis is the correct practice mode for ingraining picking habits
engine_rules.preference: do not stop to analyze mid-stroke; trust repetition to automate the pattern
engine_rules.falsifier: Pausing after every stroke to consciously verify direction interrupts the habit-formation process
engine_rules.anchor:
The
key is repetition. Do not overanalyze your right hand movements. After a short
time, these strokes will become second nature.

_provenance.section_title: Picking as habit — repetition over analysis

engine_rules.name: Players with longer alternate-picking histories face greater difficulty adopting the system
engine_rules.preference: set expectations that the habit change will take more time for advanced players
engine_rules.anchor:
The
longer you have been playing, the harder it will be to change.

_provenance.section_title: Picking as habit — repetition over analysis
